name: Dimethyltrienolone (Dimethyltren / RU-2420)

card.summary: An obscure, never-marketed trenbolone analog with reported animal potency far above methyltestosterone and no human data.
card.note: No human studies exist; described as likely severely hepatotoxic. Not approved anywhere.

quick.overview:
Dimethyltrienolone is an experimental oral anabolic steroid made in the 1960s by Roussel Uclaf. It was never sold as a medicine and has not been tested in people.

In animal assays it was reported as extremely potent, and some commentators call it one of the strongest steroids ever made. All of that rests on rodent and receptor-binding work.
quick.mechanism: It activates the androgen and progesterone receptors strongly and, like trenbolone, is not converted by aromatase or 5α-reductase. Methyl groups at two positions make it resistant to liver breakdown, allowing oral activity.
quick.risks: No human safety data exist. Reference sources describe it as expected to be highly liver-toxic and note progestogenic effects. It has no approved medical use and is available only as an unregulated research chemical.

lead: Dimethyltrienolone (RU-2420, dimethyltren) is an experimental, orally active anabolic-androgenic steroid, the 7-alpha,17-alpha-dimethyl derivative of trenbolone. It was never marketed as a medicine. In bodybuilding and muscle-building forums it is mentioned as one of the most potent anabolic compounds ever synthesised, in the context of building muscle mass for a bigger, more muscular physique.[1][2]

Wikipedia reports that in animal bioassays it had more than 100 times the anabolic and androgenic potency of methyltestosterone, that it was first described in 1967 and that it was never marketed.[1] It binds the androgen and progesterone receptors strongly and is not converted by aromatase or 5-alpha-reductase.[1][2]

No human studies exist. Wikipedia describes the compound as expected to be exceedingly hepatotoxic, and forum members discussing it commonly treat it as a reference point for extreme potency rather than a compound they report using [1][3][4]. Its closest relative, metribolone (methyltrienolone), was studied in women with advanced breast cancer in the late 1960s and early 1970s, where severe liver toxicity ended development, and it is still used as a standard research radioligand for the androgen receptor [7].

angle.text: As an anabolic steroid, it is discussed as a route to muscle growth through androgen receptor activation. Its reputation rests on animal and receptor-binding data, and no human use has been studied.

paras: Dimethyltrienolone is an agonist of the androgen receptor that also activates the progesterone receptor, so it acts as both an anabolic steroid and a progestogen. Wikipedia lists relative binding affinities of about 180 percent at the androgen receptor and 306 percent at the progesterone receptor compared with testosterone, with negligible estrogen receptor binding of about 0.1 percent.[1]

Like trenbolone, it is not a substrate for 5-alpha-reductase or aromatase, so it is not converted into more potent androgens in tissues such as prostate or skin and has no estrogenic activity.[1][2] The 17-alpha-methyl group and the 7-alpha-methyl group are described as providing oral activity and resistance to metabolism, which are also said to make it exceedingly hepatotoxic.[1][2] Human pharmacokinetic data are unavailable.[2]

Wikipedia's binding table lists relative affinities (testosterone, progesterone and other reference ligands set at 100 percent): dimethyltrienolone shows about 306 percent at the progesterone receptor, 180 at the androgen receptor, 22 at the glucocorticoid receptor and 52 at the mineralocorticoid receptor, with estrogen receptor binding of about 0.1 percent. For comparison it lists metribolone at 208 (PR) and 204 (AR), trenbolone at 74 and 197, nandrolone at 20 and 154, and testosterone at 1 and 100 [1]. The article calls its affinity among the highest known for any anabolic steroid and says it has been described as perhaps the most potent anabolic steroid ever developed, a statement it presents with animal bioassay data rather than human data [1].

Because it lacks estrogenic activity, Wikipedia says it has no propensity for estrogenic effects such as gynecomastia [1]. It is listed in androgen receptor and progesterone receptor modulator lists, and the article names related compounds including dimethyldienolone, mibolerone, trestolone and trimethyltrienolone (R-2956) [1].

It is a derivative of trenbolone carrying methyl groups at the 7-alpha and 17-alpha positions, with the triene unsaturation of the trenbolone family. The reported formula is C20H26O2 with a molar mass of about 298.4 g/mol.[2]

Wikipedia gives the systematic description 7-alpha,17-alpha-dimethyl-delta-9,11-19-nortestosterone, CAS number 10110-86-8, and states it is the 7-alpha-methyl derivative of metribolone and that it can be prepared from almestrone [1].

Wikipedia reports that dimethyltrienolone was first described in 1967, in the proceedings of a drug research symposium in Montreal, and that it was never marketed for medical use [1]. Grokipedia associates the compound with the 'RU' code series of Roussel Uclaf, a French pharmaceutical company [2].

Its relative metribolone (also called methyltrienolone or R1881) was first described in the literature in 1965 and studied in the late 1960s and early 1970s as a treatment for advanced breast cancer in women. It was effective with weak androgenicity but caused severe liver toxicity, so development stopped; by the mid-1970s it had become a standard androgen receptor ligand in research [7]. Wikipedia's metribolone article also notes that it has been encountered in sports doping and bodybuilding, and that before the 2008 Beijing Olympics 11 Greek weightlifters and 4 Greek track and field athletes tested positive for it [7].

Dimethyltrienolone has no approved status in any jurisdiction and, where it appears, is sold as a research chemical.[2] Wikipedia notes that much of what is said about its potency comes from animal bioassays, receptor-binding studies and a popular book on steroids rather than clinical work.[1]

On T Nation it appears mostly in passing. One poster raised it as an example of a compound so toxic that it might carry acute-toxicity risk, another reply urged others to stay away from a related compound after a death reported on another site, and a 2018 thread asked whether anyone had tried methyltrienolone or dimethyltrienolone.[3][4][5] Comparison tables circulated in forum threads list its receptor binding relative to other steroids.[6]

Wikipedia's metribolone article reports potency in castrated male rats of roughly 120 to 300 times the oral anabolic potency and 60 to 70 times the androgenic potency of methyltestosterone, while noting that this has not been clearly seen in human studies [7]. The same article describes the liver toxicity of metribolone as exceptionally high, attributed to its high potency and metabolic stability, with severe hepatic dysfunction in the breast cancer studies at very low doses [7]. Forum discussions of dimethyltrienolone draw on this history; one T Nation reply said people had died taking methyltrienolone, while another post, in a 2025 thread, asked whether anyone had experience with it [8][9].

No studies found. Only animal bioassays and receptor-binding experiments of the compound have been reported [1][2]. The related compound metribolone was tested in clinical studies in women with advanced breast cancer in the 1960s and 1970s and was halted for liver toxicity [7].

timeline.event: Dimethyltrienolone (RU-2420) first described from Roussel Uclaf work on nortestosterone derivatives.[1]

lore.intro: On T Nation, dimethyltrienolone is mentioned as an extreme-potency reference point more than a compound members report using.[3][4][5]

claims.claim: It is among the most potent anabolic steroids ever made
claims.believers: Forum posters cite receptor-binding comparison tables and describe it as far beyond other compounds.[6][4]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports animal potency over 100 times methyltestosterone and 180 percent androgen receptor binding relative to testosterone, with no clinical data.[1]

claims.believers: Posters describe it as far more toxic than related oral trenbolone analogs and as a possible acute-toxicity risk.[3][4]
claims.experts: Wikipedia and Grokipedia describe the compound as expected to be exceedingly hepatotoxic, based on its structure, without human data.[1][2]

claims.claim: It is a legitimate option for powerlifters who want to double their lifts
claims.believers: A T Nation post lists strong anabolic steroids, including methyltrienolone and dimethyltrienolone, as compounds that would make people very strong if used before competition, in a tone the thread frames as extreme [4].
claims.experts: No published studies have examined it in humans. Wikipedia's metribolone article reports severe liver dysfunction at very low doses in the clinical studies of the related compound [7].

claims.claim: Adding methyl groups makes steroids exponentially more potent
claims.believers: A T Nation reply explained that bolasterone is 7,17-alpha-dimethyltestosterone and compared the extra methyl group to the relationship between methyltrienolone and dimethyltrienolone, saying effects cannot be predicted from the formula [10].
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports that the 17-alpha methyl group provides oral activity and that dimethyltrienolone's binding data differ from metribolone's: higher progesterone receptor affinity and lower androgen receptor affinity [1][7].
